title: Elastic Certified Analyst
summary: The Elastic Certified Analyst (exam code ECA) is a hands-on certification for people who investigate data in the Elastic Stack, which is a search and analytics platform built around Elasticsearch for storage and Kibana for exploration. It suits SOC analysts, observability engineers and administrators who already work with logs and want proof they can answer real questions with the platform. It proves to an employer that you can bring data in, shape it, search it, build a view of it and reach a defensible conclusion under time pressure. The exam is a practical, performance-based assessment: you are given a live environment and a set of tasks, and you are graded on the artefacts you produce. It leads to security analyst, observability analyst and detection engineering roles. Elastic does not publish domain weightings, so the chapters below carry no percentages; check the vendor's current exam objectives before booking. This is an independent study guide and it is not affiliated with Elastic.

beginner.definition: The Elastic Certified Analyst is a certification from Elastic. It is about finding answers in large amounts of machine data. That data is usually logs, which are records that computers and applications write about what they did. Kibana is the web tool you use to search that data and draw charts from it. Elasticsearch is the engine that stores the data. The exam is practical rather than a written test.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many companies collect far more log data than they can actually use. Someone who can turn that data into a clear answer is valuable. Investigations and outages both depend on that skill. This certification proves the skill with a hands-on test instead of a memory test, which employers respect. It fits neatly with security operations and monitoring work. It also makes your existing Elastic experience visible on a CV.
howItWorks: Install the Elastic Stack in a lab, or use a free cloud trial. Send it some sample data to work with.
Learn how documents and fields are organised, because every search depends on that structure.
Practise the query language daily. Start with simple filters and build up to grouped statistics.
Create charts and dashboards from your own data instead of following a guided tutorial.
Rehearse timed tasks in a fresh environment, since the exam grades what you produce under a clock.
The exam itself is a set of practical tasks in a live Elastic environment. Your saved work is what gets graded.
beginner.example: Suppose your manager asks how many failed login attempts came from one office address last Tuesday. You do not read a log file by hand. You open Kibana and filter the log data by time, source address and event type. You then group the results into a chart that shows the count per hour. The answer comes from the data itself. You can also show exactly how you found it. That habit of working from evidence is what the exam rewards.
takeaways: Learn the query language well, because every task depends on it.
Build your own dashboards from your own data to gain real speed.
Practise against the clock, because time is the hardest part of the exam.

objectives: Explain how documents, fields and mappings decide what a search can and cannot find.
Bring log data into the platform from a source and confirm that the events arrived correctly.
Write queries that filter, group and summarise data to answer a specific question.
Build charts and a dashboard that let another person see the same answer quickly.
Investigate a security alert by following evidence across several event types.
Describe your findings from a dataset accurately and state the limits of what the data proves.

chapters.title: Data Ingestion and Management
objectives: Describe how documents, fields and mappings shape the queries you can run later.
Bring data from a source into the platform and confirm that the events arrived completely.
Create or adjust a data view so that colleagues can explore the same dataset.
Check data quality problems such as missing timestamps or wrong field types and describe their effect.
Explain how index patterns and retention settings affect what an investigation can still see.

chapters.title: Searching and Querying Data
objectives: Write queries that filter events by time, host, user and event type.
Use grouped aggregations to count, average and break down results by field.
Combine filters so that a broad question becomes a precise one.
Explain the difference between a full text search and an exact term match.
Save and reuse a query so that a repeated investigation becomes faster.

chapters.title: Visualization and Dashboards
objectives: Choose the chart type that shows a given result most honestly.
Build a chart from a saved query and label it so another analyst understands it.
Assemble several charts into a dashboard that answers a common operational question.
Add filters to a dashboard so that a viewer can narrow the time range or the host.
Review a dashboard and remove panels that add noise rather than insight.

chapters.title: Security Investigation and Threat Hunting
objectives: Triage a security alert by gathering the events linked to the affected host and user.
Reconstruct the sequence of activity around an alert and identify what happened first.
Search for the same behaviour on other hosts to judge how far an incident spread.
Describe a detection rule in plain language and the data it depends on.
Present an investigation conclusion with the evidence that supports it.

chapters.title: Observability Analysis
objectives: Investigate a service problem by comparing logs, metrics and traces for the same period.
Identify which component failed first when several services report errors together.
Build a view that shows the health of a service over time.
Explain how log data and metric data answer different kinds of question.
Describe the steps you would take to confirm that a problem has actually been resolved.
